analysis:
The only change in docs/architecture/inference.md is a documentation paragraph at head lines 790-806. The supplied units (head lines 818-1620) are unchanged surrounding context. The paragraph describes a new PromptTokenCache in LocalTokenizerBridge that reuses token IDs for rendered prompt pieces within the same prefix-cache scope. It also describes ChatTemplateLoopRewrites, which renders Gemma 4 and GPT-OSS templates with linear-time forms, and parallel encoding on up to four cores. The source code for these is not in the supplied evidence, so I could not verify the code behavior.

Security-relevant claims for the integration pass: (1) reuse 'never crosses a cache scope', which matters for T-041 and SEC-035, where the scope is the coordinator-authored account/model/prompt-contract salt. If the implementation keyed token reuse more broadly than that scope, it would open a cross-account timing oracle. (2) The cache holds prompt-derived token IDs in memory, so retention, eviction and persistence need checking against A-001 and T-028. The doc does not say whether this cache is persisted to disk; if it were, that would be a new at-rest artifact not covered by the DBK3/HMAC mitigations. (3) The claim that IDs equal the unchanged path's output, plus the sampled comparison that disables reuse, is an integrity assumption; a mismatch would alter the tokens the engine processes. (4) The kill switch DARKBLOOM_TTFT_PROMPT_CACHE=0 is documented. (5) The rewritten template renderers parse untrusted consumer message content, so a rendering divergence or a performance DoS is possible. None of this is verifiable from the supplied docs.

No security regression is evidenced in the documentation change itself. The threat model may need an update if PromptTokenCache is a new cross-request cache of consumer-derived data. A human or code-level reviewer should inspect PromptTokenCache.swift and the scope keying, because that code was not supplied.
